title: A Winter in Canada
text:
Last winter my aunt invited me to stay with her family in Canada for a month. I had [[never]] been [[abroad]] before, so I felt excited and a little afraid at the same time.

The flight took thirteen hours. When I [[finally]] walked out of the airport, the cold air hit my face like ice water. My aunt was waiting by the door with a thick [[coat]] for me.

Her house was [[quite]] small, but it was warm inside. My cousin Amy shared her room with me, and every morning we ate breakfast [[together]] before she went to school.

Have you [[ever]] tried to speak English all day long? By noon my ears were tired. At first I could not [[really]] follow what people said, so Amy learned to speak more slowly for me. She was patient every time I asked her to repeat something.

We went skating [[twice]] that month. The first time I fell down eleven times. The second time I fell only three times, and Amy said that was good progress for a girl from a warm island.

On the last Sunday her father drove us [[somewhere]] up in the mountains. I did not catch the name of the place. We drank hot soup out of paper cups and watched the snow come down on the [[quiet]] road. [[Maybe]] that was the best day of the whole trip.

Now I am home. My aunt's gift is [[still]] hanging by the door, and it smells a little of that cold air. When people ask me if I would go back, I say [[yes]] before they finish the question.

title: Learning to Ride
text:
My father says I was born stubborn. When I was seven, every child on our street could ride a [[bicycle]]. I could not. My legs were [[too]] short for my cousin's old bike, and I was [[afraid]] of falling.

One Saturday my father wheeled the bike out to the [[park]]. "We are [[just]] going to try," he said. "If you fall, we stop."

I fell. Then I fell [[again]], and my knee was bleeding. I said [[no]] to a third try, and my father did not argue. He [[usually]] lets me decide such things by myself.

But that night I could not sleep. I [[seldom]] give up on anything, and it made me angry to lie there thinking about it.

So we went back on Sunday, and on Monday, and after that we went [[almost]] every evening. I practiced very [[hard]]. My father ran beside me holding the seat, and he [[often]] let go without telling me.

The day I rode down the whole path by myself, I did not even know he had stopped running. I was looking [[ahead]] at the road, not behind me.

"Are you [[OK]]?" he shouted from somewhere far behind.

"I am fine!" I shouted back, and I did not stop until I reached the gate at the end of the path.

Now I ride to school every morning, and I [[always]] take the long way home past the river. My father is fifty now and his knees hurt, but he still gets his bike out when I ask him.

title: The School Play
text:
Our class decided to put on a short play for the school festival. Nobody wanted the main part, and I did [[not]] want it [[either]]. Our teacher chose me anyway.

There were forty lines to remember. At [[least]] that is what I told my mother; the true number was closer to sixty. I read them on the bus, at dinner, and [[sometimes]] in my dreams.

Two weeks before the show, our best singer moved [[away]] to Kaohsiung with her family. We had no [[music]] and only one week to find some, and we were [[so]] worried that we nearly gave the whole thing up.

[[Then]] Mr. Chen, who teaches math, told us he had played the [[guitar]] in college. He had never taken it out of its case in twenty years, and he was [[very]] slow at first. He came to practice with us after school anyway. He was [[also]] the loudest person on the stage, which made everyone laugh.

On the night of the show my hands were cold. I looked out from behind the curtain at the rows of seats. Were my parents here [[yet]]? I could see only strangers in the first three rows. [[Perhaps]] they were stuck in traffic, I thought, and I said my first line to a woman in the third row instead.

When the lights came up at the end, my mother was standing near the back door with her phone held high above her head. She had missed the beginning, but she told me later that she heard every word from the hallway.
